differential: Myasthenia Gravis

The combination of diplopia (ocular muscle weakness) and proximal limb weakness (difficulty climbing stairs) in a young woman is a classic presentation for this autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorder.

This demyelinating CNS disease is common in this demographic and can present with various neurological deficits, including diplopia from brainstem lesions and motor weakness.
Thyroid Eye Disease
Hyperthyroidism can cause both a proximal myopathy leading to weakness and an infiltrative ophthalmopathy resulting in extraocular muscle dysfunction and diplopia.
Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome
This presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder causes prominent proximal muscle weakness, and while less common than in myasthenia gravis, ocular symptoms like diplopia can also occur.
Myositis
Inflammatory myopathies cause proximal muscle weakness, which explains the difficulty climbing stairs, and can rarely involve ocular muscles leading to diplopia.
Myasthenia Gravis
The patient's age, sex, and classic symptoms of fluctuating, fatigable weakness involving ocular (ptosis, diplopia) and proximal muscles are pathognomonic for this diagnosis.
Lambert-Eaton Myasthenic Syndrome
This is another neuromuscular junction disorder that causes proximal weakness and can involve ocular muscles, though weakness classically improves briefly with exertion.
Mitochondrial Myopathy
This diagnosis can explain the combination of exercise intolerance (fatigability), ptosis, and ophthalmoplegia (causing diplopia).
Congenital Myasthenic Syndrome
These genetic disorders of the neuromuscular junction can present with a phenotype identical to autoimmune myasthenia, with some forms having onset in adulthood.
Botulism
This toxin-mediated neuromuscular blockade causes descending paralysis that often begins with cranial nerves (ptosis, diplopia), mimicking a severe myasthenic presentation.
